slides.title: You've been running at 100%.
slides.content: And calling it living. Success was supposed to be the finish line, not just the beginning of a race we never chose.
slides.notes: Hold up the mirror. Name the exhaustion of the urban trap. The average professional spends less than 2% outdoors.
slides.narrationText:
You can get very good at a life that is quietly hurting you. That’s the part nobody says out loud... uhm, because success is supposed to look clean from the outside.

But for a lot of people it doesn’t feel clean at all. It feels like calendars packed past reason, decisions made on fumes, and a body that’s always a little behind your ambition. The average professional spends less than 2% of the year outdoors, and then wonders why the weeks start to blur. See, the problem isn’t that you’re doing too little. It’s that you’ve been doing everything at full tilt for so long that full tilt has started to feel normal.

That changes how you read rest. It’s no longer a reward at the end of the month. It becomes something you have to protect, deliberately, before the year takes it away from you. Right, and once you see that, the old idea of “pushing through” starts to look less like discipline and more like drift.

This is the real tension: you don’t need another productivity trick. You need a rhythm that gives your mind and body a place to reset before they harden into exhaustion. And if 100% has become your baseline, then the first question is not how to add more. It’s what happens if you protect 10% instead... uhm, what does that actually give back to the other 90%?

slides.title: What if 10% was enough?
slides.content: 30 nights a year in the deep quiet of the wilderness. Enough time to reset your circadian rhythm. Not subtraction — protection.
slides.notes: Explain the 10% solution: 30 nights annually. A practice, not a holiday. The math of transformation.
slides.narrationText:
Because the number is smaller than the habit. That’s the whole shift. Thirty nights a year can look almost modest on paper... and still be enough to change the way your body keeps time.

Uhm, most people hear 10% and start doing arithmetic. But the point isn’t arithmetic. It’s protection. You’re not taking 90% of life and trying to squeeze rest into the cracks; you’re ring-fencing a fraction of the year so the rest doesn’t keep borrowing from it. Thirty nights across a year is enough repeated contact with deep quiet for your circadian rhythm to remember what steady feels like. Not once. Repeatedly. That matters. The body doesn’t reset because you had one beautiful weekend somewhere. It resets when it recognizes a pattern.

Right, and that’s why this isn’t a holiday logic. Holidays are what you do after depletion, when you’re already behind. This is closer to maintenance of the self. A practice. A return. If you protect 10% properly, the other 90% stops being a blur of recovery and starts becoming usable again. More focused. Less frayed. More human, actually.

So the real question is not whether you can spare 30 nights. It’s whether you can afford not to give your year a rhythm. And once you see it that way, the next question becomes very practical... what does that rhythm actually look like inside the collectives?

slides.title: Seven years of quiet work.
slides.content: 6 collectives. 1,300 acres. 250 families. We didn't just find land — we restore it. Earn trust with substance.
slides.notes: Six collectives. 1,300 acres. 250 families. Seven years. Each number as its own sentence. Regeneration, not development.
slides.narrationText:
Seven years is a long time to do quiet work without asking for applause. And that’s exactly why this matters... because the numbers here aren’t decoration, they’re evidence.

Six collectives. 1,300 acres. 250 families. Those are not abstract figures on a page. They are places that have been held, restored, and learned over time. When land has been degraded, you don’t fix it with a slogan — you bring back soil health, shade, water, native cover, the kind of long attention that actually changes what a landscape can hold. Six collectives means this isn’t a single experiment sitting on one patch of earth. It’s a pattern that has been repeated in different places, with different conditions, and kept alive. 1,300 acres means the work has scale. 250 families means there are already people living inside that pattern, not just visiting it from a distance.

Well, that’s the part people usually miss. Trust doesn’t come from the promise. It comes from substance that has survived time. Uhm, seven years is enough to know whether something is a good story or a real practice.

And once you see it that way, the shift is obvious. You’re not being asked to believe in a future idea. You’re being shown a working one. That changes the emotional risk completely... because now the question isn’t whether this can exist. The question is whether you want your 10% to sit inside something already proven.

So the next thing to ask is simple: what does it actually feel like to belong to that kind of place?

slides.title: Rewilded landscapes by Beforest.
slides.content: Poomaale 1.0 & 2.0, Coorg · Hammiyala, Coorg · Hyderabad · Bhopal · Mumbai. Belonging to a place, not just visiting.
slides.notes: Showcase the sanctuaries. Ancient forests, coffee plantations, grasslands. Not amenities — transformation.
slides.narrationText:
This is what belonging looks like when it’s real. Not a branded amenity list, not a weekend setup... a landscape that has been restored enough to hold you differently.

Poomaale in Coorg. Hammiyala in Coorg. Hyderabad. Bhopal. Mumbai. Each one is its own ecology, its own pace, its own kind of silence. Ancient forest canopy in one place, coffee and cardamom in another, grasslands in another, scrub and rock where the city gives way to something older. Well, that matters because the work here isn’t to decorate land. It’s to bring it back to life. Beforest didn’t assemble these collectives to give you a nicer backdrop. It created them so you could return to places that already have a pulse.

See, belonging changes the whole experience. You stop arriving as a consumer and start arriving as someone who knows the path, the weather, the rhythm of the place. That shift is subtle at first... then it changes how your body behaves there. You slow down sooner. You sleep differently. You notice more. And uhm, that’s not a small thing — that’s calibration.

The implication is simple. If you only ever visit nature, you stay outside it. If you keep returning to the same restored landscapes, you begin to belong to them. And once that happens, 10% of your year stops being a break from life. It becomes part of how life is held together.

So the question becomes less about where you’d go... and more about what kind of relationship you want with the land itself.

slides.title: 300 Nights of Intentional Living.
slides.content: 30 person-nights per year for 10 years. Across all Beforest Collectives. Access, not ownership. No carry-forward — rhythm, not accumulation.
slides.notes: Address objections directly. Person-nights, not family nights. Frame it as a recurring reset practice.
slides.narrationText:
And once you’ve felt the land, the structure matters. Thirty person-nights a year, for ten years... that’s the unit. Not family nights, not a loose bundle of stays — person-nights, because the practice is individual even when the people around you matter.

Across all Beforest collectives means you’re not tied to one place. Coorg, Hyderabad, the newer work as it comes online — the access moves with the network, because the point is not a single destination. It’s the rhythm of returning. And uhm, that matters more than it sounds like it does. A system like this only works if it stays alive in your calendar, not buried in your intentions.

Access, not ownership... that line does a lot of work. You’re not buying land, you’re not carrying the burden of maintaining it, and you’re not turning restoration into a private possession. You’re joining a living landscape that Beforest restores and operates. That’s a different relationship entirely. It’s cleaner, and honestly, more honest.

No carry-forward is not a restriction. It’s the discipline. If nights pile up, the practice disappears into inventory. If they reset each year, they become a reason to return, to recalibrate, to protect that time before the year swallows it.

Right, so what this really gives you is shape. A recurring reset, built into the decade, with enough room for family to participate but no confusion about what the membership is for. And the thing is... once the structure is clear, the question changes.

What would it mean to experience it first, with your feet, before you decide with your head?

slides.title: The weight of 'Next Year'.
slides.content: Every year you wait is a year of 10% you don't get back. This isn't about missing an opportunity; it's about missing a version of yourself.
slides.notes: Move away from sales urgency. Focus on the personal cost of waiting. Calibration and reset are needed now, not eventually.
slides.narrationText:
And that’s where the real cost sits... not in money, but in delay. Every year you say “next year,” you’re not just postponing a plan — you’re giving away a whole year of 10% you don’t get back.

That matters because 10% isn’t a number on a page. It’s a protected rhythm in your life, a recurring reset that makes the other 90% more usable, more steady, more human. If you wait, the work doesn’t disappear. The fatigue doesn’t disappear. The pressure just keeps collecting, and the part of you that needed recalibration keeps getting pushed further down the list. uhm, and that’s the trap — not missing a property, not missing a booking window, but missing the season when your life actually needed this most.

Well, the thing is, “next year” feels harmless when you say it once. But after a few rounds, it becomes a pattern of deferral... and patterns shape identity. You start becoming the person who always means to reset later, who always arrives tired, who always treats restoration as optional. That’s a heavier loss than any upfront decision.

So this is really about timing your life against your own exhaustion. The longer you delay, the more normal exhaustion becomes, and the harder it is to remember what a recalibrated year feels like. Right, and once you’ve lived without that rhythm long enough, you stop noticing what’s missing.

Which is why the next question isn’t whether this matters. It’s whether you want to feel it for yourself before you commit.

slides.title: Blyton Bungalow: The First 1%.
slides.content: Experience before commitment. A Kodava-inspired sanctuary built from the earth. 128 acres of private coffee forest in Coorg.
slides.notes: Details: Hospitality without the footprint. 6 signature rooms in Poomaale 1.0 where we are conserving 60 million liters of water. A place where 90-point coffee is grown. The pilot, not the backup plan. Every rupee of the trial stay will be adjusted towards membership.
slides.narrationText:
This is where it stops being an idea and becomes a place you can stand in. Blyton Bungalow is the first 1% because it’s the first time you meet the life itself, before you commit to living by it.

Uh, that matters more than it sounds like it does. The bungalow sits inside 128 acres of private coffee forest in Coorg, built with a Kodava sensibility and from the earth, not over it. It’s hospitality without the footprint — 6 signature rooms in Poomaale 1.0, while the land is being held carefully enough to conserve 60 million liters of water. And there’s a deeper signal here too: this is not ornamental nature. This is a working landscape. Coffee here has reached 90 points. The place is producing, restoring, and receiving all at once.

So the trial stay isn’t a soft entry. It’s the pilot. You come once, with your own feet on the ground, and the land tells you whether this rhythm fits you. And if it does, every rupee from that stay adjusts toward membership. No loss, no awkward second step — just a clear path if the fit is real.

Right, that changes the whole decision. You don’t have to believe the whole thing from a slide. You only have to be willing to feel whether this is the kind of life your year has been missing.

You decide with your feet, not your eyes. See you in the slow lane.
